subjects.name: Sources of Law and Courts
defs: Law based on judicial decisions resolving concrete disputes, differing from one jurisdiction to another.
Law developed through judicial decisions and precedent rather than enacted by a legislature.
The most fundamental law of a sovereign body, creating government institutions and defining the limits of their power.
A local law enacted by a municipality that carries the same force as state law where local regulation is authorized.
A doctrine in which a higher sovereign's law supersedes a lower law that would otherwise apply.
A rule made and maintained by a governmental agency exercising power delegated by a legislature.
A law enacted by a legislature, with federal statutes ultimately codified in the United States Code.
The constitutional provision making the Constitution, federal statutes, and treaties supreme law over conflicting state law.
A formally signed and ratified agreement between sovereigns that operates as federal law in the United States.
A nonparty with an interest in a case who petitions to file a brief influencing the court's decision.
The power of a court to review and correct decisions already made by lower courts.
One of twelve regional divisions of the federal system, each served by its own court of appeals.
A special appellate proceeding in which all judges of a court hear a case instead of a panel.
A court's authority to hear and decide a case first, before any appellate review.
The highest court in the federal system, holding both original and appellate jurisdiction under Article III.
An intermediate federal appellate court that reviews district court decisions for legal error without a jury.
A federal trial court that finds facts, applies law, and hears nearly all categories of federal cases.
A discretionary order directing a lower court to send its record so a higher court may review it.
A court of equity found in a few states, granting remedies such as injunctions and specific performance.
A court empowered to hear any type of case not assigned exclusively to another court.
A state's highest court, whose decisions bind every lower court in that state's system.
A court authorized to hear only particular categories of cases, such as probate or small claims.
In states that provide one, an appeals court sitting between trial courts and the court of last resort.
A specialized court that proves a will valid and supervises administration of a decedent's estate.
A state court that decides claims below a statutory dollar threshold under informal procedures.
A court created by a state constitution and statutes with authority over matters under state law.
The title used in many states for its trial-level court of general jurisdiction.
Authority shared by two or more courts to hear the same type of case.
Federal jurisdiction requiring the parties to be citizens of different states with more than $75,000 in dispute.
Federal jurisdiction over a case arising under the Constitution, federal statutes, or other federal law.
A doctrine allowing a court to decline a case because a more convenient forum can hear it.
The power of a court to adjudicate cases and issue orders, or the territory where it may act.
A court's authority to issue a binding decision against the particular party being sued.
A court's authority to decide a particular category of case and grant the remedy demanded.
The geographic place where a trial is held, fixed by statute rather than by the Constitution.
A rule stated by an appellate court that lower courts in its jurisdiction must follow.
A court's resolution of a question of law that determines the outcome of the case.
A court's adherence to its own prior decisions.
A statement in a judicial opinion that is unnecessary to the decision and therefore not binding.
A court decision treated as authority for later cases involving identical or similar facts or issues.
A doctrine requiring courts to adhere to precedent when deciding later cases with the same or related issues.
A court's adherence to decisions issued by courts higher than it in the same system.
A reference identifying a legal source that supports or relates to a statement.
A publisher's summary of an opinion's key legal points, printed ahead of the decision.
Legal authority that a court must follow because it binds within that jurisdiction.
A source of law that a court may follow but is never required to follow.
Statements of law issued by a legislature, court, or other body empowered to create binding rules.
A secondary source summarizing what the law is or what its drafters believe it should be.
Commentary about the law from sources lacking power to establish binding rules in a jurisdiction.
An exhaustive scholarly book analyzing one field of law, its principles, and its rules.

subjects.name: Civil and Criminal Procedure
defs: The body of rules that governs how courts conduct civil lawsuits, from filing through appeal.
A lawsuit in which one or more plaintiffs represent a larger group holding the same claim against a defendant.
The pleading that starts a civil case by stating the plaintiff's claims and the relief sought.
A defendant's power to move a case filed in state court into federal court when federal jurisdiction exists.
The formal delivery of a summons and complaint that gives a court authority over the defendant.
A court-issued paper commanding a defendant to appear and defend within the time stated in it.
A defendant's signed agreement to accept the summons and complaint, eliminating the need for formal service.
A defense pleaded by a defendant that, if proven, defeats liability even when the plaintiff's allegations are true.
The responsive pleading in which a defendant admits or denies each allegation and raises defenses.
A claim a defendant asserts against the plaintiff, compulsory when it arises from the same transaction.
A claim one co-party makes against another co-party arising from the same transaction as the action.
A formal request asking the court for a ruling or order, stating its grounds and the relief sought.
A pre-answer motion asserting a defect such as lack of jurisdiction or failure to state a claim.
A formal written statement of claims or defenses allowed by the rules, such as a complaint or answer.
A judgment entered without a trial when no genuine dispute of material fact exists and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
Out-of-court testimony given under oath and recorded for use in the proceeding.
The pretrial phase in which parties obtain relevant, nonprivileged information from each other to prepare for trial.
The exchange of witness names, documents, damages computations, and insurance that each party must make without a request.
Written questions one party serves on another, answered separately and under oath within thirty days.
A motion asking the court to order a discovery response after a party fails to disclose or answer.
A court order limiting or forbidding discovery to protect a person from annoyance, oppression, or undue burden.
A written request that an opposing party admit facts or the genuineness of documents, deemed admitted if unanswered.
A request that a party produce documents, electronically stored information, or tangible items within its possession or control.
A judgment entered against a defendant who failed to plead or otherwise defend after being served.
Judgment as a matter of law
A court's resolution of an issue against a party whose evidence would not let a reasonable jury find for them.
A retrial that the trial court may order on a motion filed within twenty-eight days after judgment.
An injunction granted before final judgment, issued only on notice to the adverse party.
An emergency order issued without notice when specific facts show immediate and irreparable injury before an opportunity to respond.
The jury's formal decision on the issues tried, which must be unanimous unless the parties stipulate otherwise.
The questioning of prospective jurors by a judge or lawyer to test their suitability for jury service.
A dismissal the plaintiff files without a court order, made by notice before an answer or summary judgment motion.
A request that a higher court review a lower court's determination, taken as of right or by permission.
A writ by which a higher court agrees to review a lower court's decision when review is discretionary.
A doctrine barring relitigation of an issue that a prior proceeding validly, finally, and necessarily decided.
A trial error that an appellate court refuses to reverse because it did not harm the party's right to a fair trial.
An appeal from a non-final order entered while the case is still proceeding in the trial court.
An appellate court's return of a case to the lower court to reconsider or retry in light of its ruling.
A doctrine barring a second lawsuit over the same cause of action after a final judgment on the merits.
The level of scrutiny an appellate court applies when reviewing a lower court's ruling.
A resolution of the charged offense's factual elements in the defendant's favor, absolving the defendant from the accusation.
The open-court proceeding where the defendant receives the charging document and is asked to enter a plea.
A judge's order authorizing an arrest, issued when a complaint and its affidavits establish probable cause.
A group of sixteen to twenty-three citizens who decide whether the prosecutor's evidence supports an indictment.
A grand jury's written charge formally accusing a person of a crime, required for federal felonies.
A prosecutor's written criminal charge filed without a grand jury after the defendant waives indictment.
The defendant's first court appearance after arrest, when the court advises the defendant of rights and charges.
An agreement under which a defendant pleads guilty in exchange for the prosecutor's recommendation or a reduced charge.
A hearing at which a magistrate judge decides whether probable cause supports the charge.

subjects.name: Constitutional Rights
defs: The first ten constitutional amendments, which enumerate protections for speech, religion, jury trial, and limits on searches and punishment.
Constitutional freedoms that limit how government may treat individuals, such as speech, religion, and the press.
An Eighth Amendment punishment that is excessive relative to the offense or inflicted as deliberate suffering.
The judiciary's power to examine legislative and executive acts and invalidate them as unconstitutional.
The provision recognizing an individual right to keep and bear arms for lawful purposes, subject to permissible regulation.
Rights retained by the people that the Constitution's list does not name, safeguarded by the Ninth Amendment.
A speech regulation that classifies expression by its message or subject matter, triggering the highest level of judicial scrutiny.
The First Amendment provision barring government-established religion and any undue preference for religion or nonreligion.
The First Amendment clause reserving to individuals the right to practice the religious beliefs and rituals they choose.
The First Amendment right to speak, write, and share ideas without government punishment, subject to recognized exceptions.
The First Amendment right to publish and report information through any medium without government censorship.
A government restriction blocking expression before it happens, such as a license requirement or injunction, which courts disfavor strongly.
A neutral rule governing when, where, or how expression occurs that leaves open alternative channels of communication.
Government favoritism toward one perspective on a subject, treated as a particularly disfavored form of content discrimination.
The Fifth and Fourteenth Amendment guarantee that the government deprives no person of life, liberty, or property without due process of law.
The requirement that government operates within established law and gives fair procedures whenever it acts against an individual.
A due process requirement that a party receive meaningful warning of a proceeding that may affect their rights.
The constitutional demand for notice, a hearing, and a neutral decision-maker before the government deprives someone of protected interests.
A constitutional liberty against government intrusion into personal decisions, derived by courts from several amendments.
The doctrine shielding fundamental rights from government interference regardless of the procedures the government follows.
A ruling invalidating a law whose text fails to give ordinary people clear notice of what conduct it forbids.
Legal entitlements enacted by law that secure equal treatment and protection from discrimination.
The requirement that government apply its laws fairly and treat people in similar situations alike without an unjustified distinction.
A right that, when burdened by government action, moves judicial review to the strict scrutiny standard.
A mid-level review requiring an important government interest pursued by means substantially related to that interest.
A group of people whom statutes shield from discrimination based on traits such as race, sex, religion, age, or disability.
The most permissive review, upholding a law with a legitimate purpose and a rational link between that purpose and its means.
The most demanding review, which requires a narrowly tailored means serving a compelling government interest.
A classification targeting a historically disfavored group, such as race or national origin, that receives strict judicial scrutiny.
The Fifth Amendment protection against being prosecuted or punished twice for the same offense.
A rule barring the government from introducing most evidence obtained in violation of the Constitution at trial.
A court order requiring a custodian to produce a detained person so a judge may determine whether the confinement is lawful.
The advisement police give before custodial questioning, covering silence, counsel, and the use of statements as evidence.
A fair probability, based on facts and circumstances, that a crime occurred or evidence exists in a particular place.
A criminal defendant's Sixth Amendment right to a lawyer's assistance, including appointed counsel for those who cannot pay.
Government examination of a person or property for evidence and the taking of items, which the Fourth Amendment requires to be reasonable.
A judge-issued authorization for an arrest, search, or seizure, supported by probable cause and a sworn description.
A system dividing governing power between a national government and smaller units that each retain authority over local concerns.
A doctrine applying most Bill of Rights protections to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause.
A defense shielding government officials from damages suits unless they violate a clearly established statutory or constitutional right.
The Court's approach of applying individual Bill of Rights guarantees to the states piece by piece rather than wholesale.
Conduct taken by the government, or private conduct so connected to the government that it counts as official action.
Conduct carried out under the appearance of legal authority, including official acts that exceed or misuse granted power.

subjects.name: Contracts
defs: An offeree's assent to an offer's terms, expressed in words or shown by conduct.
A contract in which each party's promise serves as consideration for the other's promise.
A reply that rejects the original offer while proposing a new one on different terms.
Under UCC Article 2, a merchant's signed promise to hold a goods offer open without consideration.
A common-law doctrine requiring acceptance to match the offer exactly, with no changed or added terms.
Agreement by all parties to a contract, judged by their outward expressions rather than private thoughts.
A proposal to be bound on stated terms if the other party accepts it.
A supported promise to keep an offer open for a set time, during which the offeror cannot revoke.
A contract that the offeree accepts only by performing the act the offer calls for.
A doctrine that courts leave the fairness of the value exchanged to the parties themselves.
A person's legal ability to make binding contracts, requiring minimum age and sound mind.
Something of value each party gives or promises to induce the other party's promise.
A gift promise that binds no one because nothing is exchanged for it.
A promise so vague or conditional that it leaves the promisor bound to nothing.
A doctrine that lets a minor avoid contracts because minors are presumed to lack capacity.
A rule that performance already owed supplies no consideration for a promise to pay more.
A doctrine enforcing a promise without consideration when reasonable reliance would otherwise work injustice.
An otherwise valid contract that one protected party may choose to disaffirm.
A standardized form drafted by the stronger party and offered on a take-it-or-leave-it basis.
Coercion through unlawful threats that destroys free will and makes a contract voidable.
A formation requirement that a contract's purpose be lawful before a court will enforce it.
A false statement or misleading omission made to induce another party's reliance.
A shared false belief about a basic assumption that may make a contract voidable.
A rule barring prior or contemporaneous agreements offered to contradict an integrated written contract.
A rule requiring a signed writing for land sales, one-year contracts, and goods priced at $500 or more.
A defense of unfair bargaining combined with oppressive terms that lets a court refuse enforcement.
Excessive persuasion by a trusted party that overcomes free will and makes a contract voidable.
Under UCC Article 2, refusing performance before it is due in a way that impairs the contract's value.
A party's failure to perform a promised duty without a legal excuse.
An event that must occur before a party's duty to perform begins.
An event that, once it occurs, terminates a duty already owed under the contract.
A defense excusing performance when an unforeseen event makes it excessively difficult or expensive.
A failure that defeats a contract's essential purpose and allows the injured party to end the contract.
Under UCC Article 2, a buyer may reject goods that fail in any respect to conform.
A party's clear statement or conduct showing an intention not to perform a contractual obligation.
Performance that fulfills a contract's core purpose despite minor deviations, leaving only a claim for damages.
Losses from a breach that the breaching party had reason to know would follow it.
Damages that put the non-breaching party in as good a position as full performance would have.
A contract term fixing a reasonable sum for breach where actual loss would be hard to prove.
Recovery of expenditures reasonably incurred in relying on a promise that was later broken.
A remedy canceling a contract and restoring both parties to their pre-agreement positions.
A remedy restoring the value of benefits conferred on the other party to prevent unjust enrichment.
A court order compelling the promised act when money damages cannot repair the harm.

subjects.name: Torts
defs: A defendant's failure to conform to the standard of care that the law requires in the circumstances.
Factual causation established by a but-for test linking the defendant's conduct to the plaintiff's harm.
An obligation to act reasonably to avoid harming others, forming the first element of a negligence claim.
An obligation to help a person in peril that arises when one's own conduct created the danger.
A measure of whether a reasonable person could have predicted the harm resulting from the defendant's conduct.
A civil wrong in which a person fails to exercise the care a reasonable person would under similar circumstances.
A legally sufficient cause that ties the defendant's breach to harm within the range of foreseeability.
An objective test asking how a hypothetical person of ordinary prudence would act in the same situation.
Negligence established automatically by violating a statute designed to protect people from the type of harm suffered.
A presumption of negligence arising when an accident ordinarily occurs only through carelessness while the causing object was under the defendant's control.
An intentional act that causes another person to reasonably apprehend imminent harmful or offensive contact.
An intentional harmful or offensive contact with a person without consent, needing no proof of actual loss.
A false statement of fact published to a third party that harms the subject's reputation.
An intentional restraint that confines a person within a bounded area without consent or legal authority.
Outrageous conduct done intentionally or recklessly that causes another person severe emotional distress.
A civil wrong committed purposefully, requiring proof of intent rather than mere carelessness.
A tort protecting private life, encompassing intrusion on seclusion, public disclosure of private facts, false light, and appropriation.
Defamation expressed in written or otherwise recorded form rather than in speech.
Defamation communicated through spoken words rather than in a fixed or recorded form.
An uncommon activity creating a very significant risk of physical harm even when all parties exercise reasonable care.
A dangerous artificial condition on land that draws trespassing children who cannot appreciate the risk.
A design-defect standard finding no liability when an ordinary consumer would not expect the product to be defective.
A flaw inherent in a product's plan before manufacture, making the product unreasonably dangerous as designed.
A product defect created by inadequate instructions or missing warnings about latent dangers.
A flaw confined to some units of a product line, arising during construction rather than in the design.
Responsibility of commercial sellers in a product's chain for injuries caused by a defective product they place in commerce.
A design-defect standard excusing a defendant when a product's usefulness outweighs its inherent risk of harm.
Liability imposed without regard to the defendant's intent or care when the law deems the activity inherently risky.
Money awarded equal to the plaintiff's proven loss, intended to restore rather than punish.
Money a court orders paid to make an injured party whole for a proven civil wrong.
Harm that flows directly and inevitably from the wrong, suffered by any injured party in that situation.
A doctrine barring recovery of losses the injured party could have avoided through reasonable efforts.
A token sum, such as one dollar, that acknowledges a violated legal right with no measurable loss.
Extra money awarded alongside compensatory damages to punish intentional or wanton misconduct and deter repetition.
Quantifiable losses with a set monetary cost, such as medical bills or property repair expenses.
A statutory award of three times the proven actual damages, imposed for especially egregious conduct.
A common-law defense that bars recovery when a plaintiff voluntarily accepted the known danger, merged into comparative negligence in many jurisdictions.
A rule reducing a plaintiff's recovery by the plaintiff's own share of fault instead of barring it outright, in pure or modified forms.
A voluntary agreement to another's proposed conduct, requiring capacity and an absence of coercion, fraud, or error.
A common-law rule barring any recovery by a plaintiff who was even slightly negligent, retained in four states and the District of Columbia.
Reasonable force used to protect a third party from another person's threatened or attempted force.
A rule making a volunteer rescuer who takes charge of a helpless person liable for negligent care in the rescue.
A doctrine letting a negligent plaintiff recover when the defendant had the final opportunity to avoid the harm.
Force reasonably believed necessary to repel an imminent unlawful attack, limited to a proportionate response.
A common-law doctrine preventing suits against the government unless it consents, with federal and state waivers available by statute.

subjects.name: Criminal Law
defs: The physical element of a crime, consisting of a voluntary act or a chargeable omission.
The element that connects the defendant's conduct to the prohibited result, proven as but-for or proximate cause.
Proof that the essential parts of the charged crime actually occurred, required before a prosecution proceeds.
A crime treated as inherently wrong under general community standards, such as murder.
A crime that statutes prohibit although it is not inherently wrong, such as a parking violation.
A failure to act that satisfies actus reus only when a legal duty to act existed.
An actual cause that is also legally sufficient to support criminal liability for the result.
Intent aimed at one victim that supplies the mental state for harm to a different victim.
A bodily movement the defendant controls, excluding reflexes and convulsions from actus reus.
An intent to perform the prohibited act without a wish for its consequences.
A Model Penal Code mental state in which the defendant is practically certain the conduct causes the result.
The common-law mental state for murder, satisfied by intent to kill or harm, felony murder, or depraved heart.
The culpable state of mind a prosecutor must prove, such as purpose, knowledge, recklessness, or negligence.
A Model Penal Code mental state in which a defendant is unaware of a risk a careful person would notice.
A Model Penal Code mental state in which the defendant has a conscious object to bring about the result.
A Model Penal Code mental state in which the defendant consciously disregards a substantial and unjustified risk.
An intent to bring about a particular result beyond simply performing the prohibited act.
An offense that requires proof of the act but no proof of any guilty state of mind.
A common-law offense of intentionally putting another person in reasonable apprehension of imminent harmful or offensive contact.
An inchoate offense requiring intent to commit the target crime, plus dangerous proximity at common law or a substantial step under the Model Penal Code.
A common-law offense of intentionally causing harmful or offensive physical contact with another person without consent.
Unlawful entry into a building with intent to commit a crime inside, though the exact elements vary by jurisdiction.
An agreement between two or more people to commit an illegal act, plus intent and an overt act in most jurisdictions.
A rule that treats a death occurring during a dangerous felony as murder without any intent to kill.
The negligent causing of another person's death, a killing punished as a lesser offense than murder.
The common-law taking of another person's property with the intent to deprive the owner of it.
An unlawful killing of another person with malice aforethought, graded into degrees by most modern statutes.
The unlawful taking of property from a person or their presence by force or threat of force.
An intentional killing without malice, charged for heat of passion at common law or extreme disturbance under the Model Penal Code.
A criminal justification permitting reasonable force to protect another person from an imminent unlawful attack.
A claim that mental impairment prevented the specific intent required, reducing the charge instead of producing an acquittal.
A defense that a reasonable threat of imminent death or serious bodily injury compelled the criminal act.
A defense that exempts the defendant from liability without claiming the conduct itself was justified.
A defense that mental disease left the defendant unable to know wrongfulness or, under the Model Penal Code, to appreciate or conform.
A defense that intoxication prevented the required mental state, with involuntary intoxication accepted more readily than voluntary.
A defense claiming the conduct itself was right or warranted, so punishment serves no purpose.
A defense that illegal conduct was the lesser of two evils, with no reasonable alternative and no greater danger created.
A criminal justification permitting reasonable and proportionate force to repel an imminent unlawful attack on oneself.
The death penalty imposed by a state as punishment for a crime and carried out by execution.
Advisory rules that federal judges consult to calculate a sentence from offense seriousness and criminal history.
The imprisonment range found by intersecting a defendant's offense level with their criminal history category.
A minimum penalty set by statute that leaves the sentencing judge no discretion to go lower.
Conditional release from prison before the sentence is fully served, subject to supervision and conditions.
A sentence of community supervision in place of incarceration, imposed with conditions set by the court.
An offender's tendency to commit new crimes that produce fresh convictions after a prior sentence.
The stage at which a court imposes a penalty on a defendant after conviction.
A period of court supervision that follows a federal prison sentence to support the offender's return to the community.
A sentencing structure that mandates a life term upon a third serious or violent felony conviction.
